holidays.name: Johnny Appleseed Day
holidays.description: A day to honor America's best-known apple evangelist. Celebrate with apple pie, cider, or a fresh apple tree, and maybe a pot on your head for the full look.
holidays.origin: The day marks the birthday of John Chapman, born September 26, 1774, in Massachusetts. He became a folk hero for planting apple nurseries across the American frontier in the early 1800s.
holidays.funFact: Most of Johnny Appleseed's apples were small and tart, and they were grown mainly for hard cider, not for eating. The cider was the real prize for frontier settlers.

holidays.name: National Chimichanga Day
holidays.description: A salute to the deep-fried burrito. It is crispy, golden, and smothered in cheese, salsa, and sour cream. Today is a good day to skip the diet.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial food observance. The chimichanga is usually linked to Arizona's Southwest border cuisine. Tucson's El Charro Café says its founder accidentally dropped a burrito into hot oil there.
holidays.funFact: According to the El Charro legend, the founder started to shout a curse word when the burrito hit the oil. She swapped in the playful Spanish word 'chimichanga,' which roughly means 'thingamajig.'

holidays.name: National Dumpling Day
holidays.description: A day for pillowy, stuffed, steamed, boiled, or fried little pockets of joy. Pierogi, gyoza, empanadas, and matzo balls all count.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance of unclear origin. It lets dumpling fans of every cuisine celebrate their favorite comfort food.
holidays.funFact: Nearly every food culture has its own dumpling. Examples include Chinese jiaozi, Polish pierogi, Italian gnocchi, Georgian khinkali, and Nepalese momos.
